newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: OECD warns of S.Korean currency problems.
newsitem.headline: OECD warns of S.Korean currency problems.

text.p: South Korea's currency, the won, could come under pressure unless inflation starts slowing next year, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said on Thursday.
"The principal risk to the economy stems from its increased exposure to world capital markets," the OECD said in a semi-annual report.

Large capital inflows, indicating overseas investor confidence, may be affected if inflation does not show clear signs of slowing next year, the Paris-based think tank said in its annual report on member economies.
"Any slackening of the rate of foreign investment, unmatched in the short term by a fall in the current account deficit, might generate pressure on the exchange rate."

Heavy inflows on the capital account, mainly into the stock market, are now more than covering a large current account deficit, which will exceed $20 billion this year, or 4.4 percent of gross domestic product.

Consumer inflation was at 4.3 percent for the first 11 months of this year, although unofficial estimates put the real figure in double digits. The target for the full year is below 4.5 percent against 4.7 percent last year.
The won has lost about eight percent against the dollar this year. But it has gained about one percent against the yen, reflecting the steeper fall of the yen against the dollar.

South Korea argues it cannot afford to liberalise its financial markets too quickly -- in particular the bond market -- for fear that sudden currency inflows will put upward pressure on the currency and stoke inflation.
Inflation, in turn, would drive away foreign investment.

The report said falling export prices for semiconductors, steel and petrochemicals plus slack investment and consumption will keep economic growth at 6.6 percent in 1996 after two years of nine percent growth.

Growth is forecast at the same level in 1997. However, easing interest rates and a cheaper won starting in late 1997 and continuing into 1988 could lead to a spurt of growth, pushing the rate of GDP expansion back to 7.0 percent.

"As profits are depressed, investment, especially by semiconductor manufacturers, should show little increase. With consumption growth also likely to slacken as employment growth starts to weaken no pick up in GDP growth is envisaged in 1997 as a whole," it said.
South Korea was invited in October to become the 29th member of the OECD and the second Asian country after Japan. It formally entered this month.
